opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So this is a debate I spent a lot of time on during my PhD, and I think the history is illuminating.

In the early-to-mid twentieth century, a lot of thinking about technology was broadly what we'd now call technologically determinist. Thinkers like Marx, at least in some readings, or Lynn White with his famous argument about the stirrup and feudalism, or later people like Jacques Ellul, saw technology as a powerful, almost autonomous force. Technology develops according to its own logic, and society more or less has to adapt to it. The hand mill gives you the feudal lord; the steam mill gives you the industrial capitalist.

Then, starting around the 1970s and 80s, there was a strong reaction against that in science and technology studies. Social constructivists like Trevor Pinch and Wiebe Bijker, with their work on the bicycle, argued that technologies don't have a single inevitable trajectory. What counts as a "working" technology is negotiated among relevant social groups. Interests, culture, and politics shape which designs win out. The lesson was: technology is a human product, so we shouldn't treat it as an external force acting on us.

I think that reaction was partly healthy. Crude determinism can be fatalistic and can hide the choices people are actually making. It also lets powerful actors say, "This is just progress, you can't stop it."

But I think the pendulum swung too far. In much of the field, "technological determinism" became something of an insult, a position nobody wanted to be caught holding. And that made it harder to talk about something that I think is clearly real: that at the macro level, over long time spans and across competing societies, technology does have a lot of structuring power. If a technology confers big economic or military advantages, the groups that adopt it tend to outcompete the groups that don't. That creates strong selection pressures. So individual actors and local decisions matter a great deal for the details, but there are also these broad currents that are very hard for any single actor to resist.

So the way I'd put it is that both perspectives are partly right at different levels of analysis. Social constructivism is often right at the micro level: specific designs, specific adoption paths, who benefits. A kind of soft or structural determinism is often right at the macro level: competition and the advantages a technology confers shape the long-run trajectory of civilization.

And that matters a lot for thinking about AI. If you're purely constructivist, you might think we can just collectively decide what AI becomes. If you're purely determinist, you might think governance is pointless. I think the truth is in between: there are powerful competitive pressures pushing in certain directions, and good governance means understanding those pressures clearly so we can find the points of leverage where human choice actually can steer things.

r001.rationale: It describes technology as an almost autonomous force that develops according to its own logic while society adapts.

r002.rationale: It says crude determinism can hide the choices people are making and stresses that individual actors and local decisions matter.

r003.rationale: It says technologies have no single inevitable trajectory and that their designs are shaped through negotiation among social groups.

r004.rationale: It says technological determinism became an insult, but does not say social constructivist scholars treated it as a straw man constructed by critics.

r005.rationale: It criticizes the field for making it harder to discuss technology’s broad structuring power, but does not connect that dismissal to a turn toward micro-level histories.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I spent a lot of time on earlier in my career, and I think it's actually quite important for how we think about AI today.

The story usually gets told as a kind of pendulum. If you go back to the early and mid-twentieth century, the dominant framing in a lot of history and social science was broadly deterministic: technology has its own logic, it develops along a fairly fixed trajectory, and then society has to adapt to it. You see this in Marx to some extent — "the hand-mill gives you society with the feudal lord, the steam-mill, society with the industrial capitalist" — and in people like Lynn White on the stirrup and feudalism, or Ogburn's idea of "cultural lag," where institutions are always scrambling to catch up with the machines.

Then starting in the seventies and eighties there was a very strong reaction against that, mostly out of sociology and history of science. This is the social construction of technology school — Bijker, Pinch, Hughes, MacKenzie, and others. Their point was: look closely at any actual technology and you find that its form wasn't inevitable at all. The bicycle could have gone several ways. Nuclear weapons accuracy wasn't just a function of physics; it was driven by particular organisational interests in the US Navy and Air Force. So technology is shaped by politics, culture, who's funding it, what problems people think are worth solving. And "technological determinism" became almost a slur — a sign that you hadn't done your homework.

And I think that critique was largely correct as a description of the micro-level. At the scale of a particular artefact, a particular firm, a particular decade, there's a huge amount of contingency and social shaping.

But my view is that the pendulum swung too far, and in a way that's actually unhelpful. If you zoom out — to the scale of centuries, of competing societies, of the whole system rather than individual actors — a lot of the contingency washes out. The reason is selection. Societies and organisations that adopt more effective technologies tend to outcompete, absorb, or get imitated by those that don't. So even if no single actor is "forced" to build the steam engine or the rifle or the semiconductor, the system as a whole ends up looking as though it were. I've called this "military-economic adaptationism": competition acts as a filter, and over the long run the filter produces something that looks like a deterministic trajectory, even though every individual step was socially constructed.

So the way I'd put it is: determinism and constructivism are answers to slightly different questions, at different scales. Constructivism is right that any given actor has choices. The determinists were pointing at something real about what happens when you aggregate lots of actors under competitive pressure. The interesting question isn't "which one is true," it's "under what conditions does social choice actually get to bind, and under what conditions does competition erode it?"

And that's exactly why I think this matters for AI. A lot of AI governance is implicitly a bet that we're in the constructivist regime — that we can shape what gets built, how fast, with what safeguards. The deterministic worry is that competitive pressure between labs, between countries, will select for whoever cuts the most corners, and our choices get washed out. My sense is that neither extreme is right, but the honest version of the governance project is: identify where the selection pressure is strong, and try to change the structure of competition itself — through coordination, norms, institutions — rather than just hoping individual actors will choose well.

r001.rationale: It describes earlier deterministic views in which technology follows its own logic and society adapts to it.

r002.rationale: It says that examining actual technologies reveals choices shaped by politics, culture, funding, and perceived problems, making the social decisions behind technological history visible.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says a technology’s form was not inevitable and that its development is socially shaped.

r004.rationale: It says technological determinism became a slur, but does not say constructivist scholars treated it as a straw man they had constructed.

r005.rationale: It argues that the pendulum swung too far and restores a role for competition at large scales, but does not state that micro-level histories led scholars to dismiss technology’s profound effects on society.

astra-6.text:
I’d describe it as a shift in where we look for explanations. Technological determinism treats technology as having something like its own trajectory: inventions arrive, and then society adapts to their consequences. In its strongest form, technology is the driving force, and social arrangements are largely downstream of it.

Social constructivism pushes back by asking: Why did this particular technology get developed? Who funded it? Whose problems was it designed to solve? There are often multiple possible designs, and the selection among them depends on institutions, interests, and people’s interpretations of what the technology is for. So technology is itself something we need to explain, rather than simply taking it as an external cause.

I think that’s a valuable corrective, but you can push it too far. The fact that a technology is socially shaped doesn’t mean its physical properties don’t constrain what happens next. A useful account needs both directions: society shapes which technologies emerge, and those technologies then change the opportunities and constraints facing society.

r001.rationale: It describes technology as having its own trajectory and, in the strongest form, as the driving force behind social change.

r002.rationale: It pushes back by asking who funded and designed a technology and whose problems it served, making the people and decisions behind technology part of the explanation.

r003.rationale: It says there are multiple possible designs and that institutions, interests, and interpretations shape which one is selected.

r004.rationale: It does not say that social constructivist scholars treated technological determinism as a straw man created by critics.

r005.rationale: It says technology’s physical properties constrain what happens next, but does not convey that micro-level histories led scholars to dismiss technology’s profound effects on society.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the shift was, in part, a reaction to the idea that technology develops according to its own internal logic, and then society simply adapts to it. On that technological determinist view, you might say that industrialisation produces a particular kind of political order, or that a particular military technology inevitably changes the balance of power.

Social constructivists pushed back by asking: Why did this technology develop in this particular way? Who funded it? What problems were its designers trying to solve? And how did different groups interpret and use it? Once you ask those questions, you see that things we might treat as technical necessities often reflect social choices, institutions, and distributions of power.

But I don’t think we should go from saying that technology determines everything to saying that technology has no independent effects. Technologies create real capabilities and constraints. The useful position is that the relationship runs both ways: society shapes which technologies emerge and how they’re used, and those technologies then reshape the possibilities available to society. The challenge is to understand where there’s room for choice, and where the material properties of a technology make some outcomes more likely than others.

r001.rationale: It describes the determinist view as technology developing by its own internal logic while society adapts, and gives examples of technology shaping political order and power.

r002.rationale: It says the critique asks who funded a technology and what its designers sought to solve, bringing human decisions into technological history.

r003.rationale: It says technologies emerge through social choices, institutions, and power, and asks why a technology developed in a particular way—making its form contingent.

r004.rationale: It does not say social constructivists regarded technological determinism as a straw man constructed by critics.

r005.rationale: It does not report that micro-level histories led scholars to dismiss technology’s profound social effects; instead, it affirms that technologies have real effects.
